hints: Intersect: $-x + 6 = \frac{1}{3}x + 2 \implies x = 3, y = 3 \implies (3,3)$ lies on $y = x$.
walkthrough:
Find the $x$-coordinates of $P$ and $Q$ by setting $y = 4$:
$$\frac{x}{2} + \frac{6}{x} = 4 \implies x^2 - 8x + 12 = 0 \implies (x - 2)(x - 6) = 0$$
$$x = 2 \implies P(2, \, 4), \quad x = 6 \implies Q(6, \, 4)$$

Find the derivative and tangent gradients at $P$ and $Q$:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{6}{x^2}$$
$$\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=2} = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{6}{4} = -1, \quad \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=6} = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{6}{36} = \frac{1}{3}$$

Form the equations of both tangent lines:
$$\text{Tangent at } P: \quad y - 4 = -1(x - 2) \implies y = -x + 6$$
$$\text{Tangent at } Q: \quad y - 4 = \frac{1}{3}(x - 6) \implies y = \frac{1}{3}x + 2$$

Solve simultaneously for the intersection point of the tangents:
$$-x + 6 = \frac{1}{3}x + 2 \implies \frac{4}{3}x = 4 \implies x = 3$$
$$y = -3 + 6 = 3 \implies (3, \, 3)$$
$$\text{Since the point is } (3, 3), \text{ it lies on the line } y = x$$

Set up the volume of revolution integral for the region between $y = 4$ and $y = \frac{x}{2} + \frac{6}{x}$ from $x = 2$ to $x = 6$:
$$V = \pi \int_2^6 \left[ 4^2 - \left(\frac{x}{2} + \frac{6}{x}\right)^2 \right]\,dx$$

Evaluate the definite integral between the limits $x = 2$ and $x = 6$:
$$\text{At } x = 6: \quad 10(6) - \frac{6^3}{12} + \frac{36}{6} = 60 - 18 + 6 = 48$$
$$\text{At } x = 2: \quad 10(2) - \frac{2^3}{12} + \frac{36}{2} = 20 - \frac{2}{3} + 18 = 38 - \frac{2}{3} = \frac{112}{3}$$
$$V = \pi \left( 48 - \frac{112}{3} \right) = \frac{32\pi}{3} \quad \left(\text{or } 10\frac{2}{3}\pi \approx 33.5\right)$$
